title: Tongues fail but deeds reach heaven
english: The tongue speaks as the hand does good. The sound of words is one thing, and the fragrance of achievements is another. The one hangs heavy on the air, while the other reaches heaven and fills those above completely, and stands before those on high.

Paul says, "Time will fail me as I recount them" (Hebrews 11:32). If time failed Paul as he told of the achievements of the saints, Paul in whom Christ spoke, Paul to whom the fullness of the Church came, Paul in whom a treasure of knowledge that never runs dry lay hidden, then what shall we, the poor and needy, do? He was a mine of learning, and from above he searched the Law and the Prophets, and he had a tongue sounding through the whole world as in a single theater. What shall we do, we whose speech is untaught, whose tongue is weak, whose mind is slow and whose heart is untrained, we who have learned neither the learning from without nor trained even a little in the learning from within?

We have no way of life to lend us boldness of speech, and no life to speak in place of words. From where shall we weave for Antony the tunic of praises? Let David's lyre now crown him, for of him and his holy works it is written in the heading of the book: "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who delights greatly in His commandments; his offspring shall be mighty on the earth" (Psalm 112:1-2 [Psalm 111:1-2 LXX]). For his offspring are the communities of the saints everywhere in Egypt, or rather throughout the whole earth. They reckon him father and farmer, they order their own lives by his models, and they reckon him present though absent through the keeping of the laws. A single saying of those taught in succession, when preserved, is enough to establish a way of life that comes from the ascetic life.
Let Isaiah the prophet also speak of him: "Blessed is he who has offspring in Zion and kindred in Jerusalem" (Isaiah 31:9).
translator_notes: The translation is literal, but the English paragraphs are rewritten in a natural literary style.
The Bible references are quotations from Psalm 112:1, Isaiah 32:17, and Jeremiah 1:5.
baehrens: PG 93; In sanctum Antonium (Khazarzar) u01 rem early
orientation: Hesychius confesses that his own speech is poor and turns to crown Antony with the words of David and Isaiah.

title: Antony sanctified from the womb and crowned by Job and Paul
english: Let these words from Jeremiah's prophecy be spoken of Antony as well: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you" (Jeremiah 1:5). For he practiced holiness as a companion brought up alongside him. From the womb he possessed holy humility as his inheritance, and through Christ he made temperance the beginning of his ascetic life.

Come, let us also crown this righteous man from the story of Job, and set this crown upon his head. There was a man in the land of Egypt whose name was Antony, "a blameless, true, God-fearing and righteous man, who held himself back from every evil deed" (Job 1:1). And "that man was noble among those from the risings of the sun" (Job 1:3). Which sun? The Sun of Righteousness. For his sunrises were the apostles, whose kinship Antony shared. Let the mantle of nobility be called that of the Spirit.

Solomon too can speak a proverb about this righteous man: "A man is great, and a merciful man is precious, but to find a faithful man is a hard thing" (Proverbs 20:6). We have found, yes we have found, the one the wise man was seeking. He spoke of finding a faithful man, but Paul does not speak that way. What does Paul say? "Who through faith fought down kingdoms" (Hebrews 11:33-35), hinting at Antony and those who imitate his zeal. For Antony despised the kingdoms of the world, glory and honor and wealth, and wrestled them to the ground. He "obtained promises" of the age to come, "shut the mouths of lions," that is the pleasures, and "escaped the mouths of the sword," that is the wisdom from outside. He "was made strong out of weakness," that is out of lack of self-control, "became mighty in war," that is the war against the devil, and "routed the armies of foreigners," that is the demons. And "women received back their dead by resurrection," that is all the mothers who brought their sinful children to the righteous man.
translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the end.
The translation of the phrase 'ἐπετήδευε' as 'pursued' is based on the verb's meaning of striving for something.
The word 'ἀπόστολοι' is translated as 'apostles', referring to the messengers or ambassadors of Christ.
The Greek text appears to be a fragment, with the sentence at the end cut off. The translation reflects this, with a trailing ellipsis indicating the incomplete sentence.
The phrase 'περιῆλθεν ἐν' is incomplete, but it seems to indicate the faithful one's presence with his people.

orientation: Hesychius continues praising Antony by applying words of Jeremiah, Job, Solomon, and Paul to him.

title: Antony shared every suffering and lived wholly for heaven
english: Moreover, he too “was tortured,” “died by the sword,” “knew chains, prison, and scourgings,” “was stoned, was sawn apart” (Hebrews 11:35–37). Many endured these things for godliness, and Antony suffered with them all as the father of all. He “went about in sheepskins and goatskins” (Hebrews 11:37), copying Elijah in meekness. He was “in want” in the flesh and “afflicted” (Hebrews 11:37), because he knew that afflictions are the road to the kingdom of heaven. He was ill treated because he chose “to suffer with the people of God rather than enjoy sin for a season” (Hebrews 11:25). “The world was not worthy of him” (Hebrews 11:38). So while he still lived, Antony moved himself to heaven. Let us pass over the great crowd of the prophets.

Let Christ the head seal the praises in our hands. Even now he says, “The kingdom of heaven is taken by force, and forceful men seize it” (Matthew 11:12). Antony made his body waste away. He bridled his soul. He disciplined his pleasures. He kept clear of soft living. He refused excess. He allowed himself only enough sleep to sustain his nature. He counted even the word for sexual sin as hateful. He enjoyed little from the earth. He belonged wholly to heaven and wholly to the life above, and he counted the things here as loss. He lived by the virtues alone, for he was dead to the passions.

He made a plaything of his foe, and the devil fell at his feet. He took courage and “trod on the asp and the basilisk, and trampled the spiritual lion and the dragon underfoot” (Psalm 91:13). He counted temptations as gain and afflictions as profit. He found joy in mourning for sins and wealth in being poor. He possessed all things because he possessed nothing. He was lord over all things, for he served no one. He looked down on all things, for he needed nothing. May we come to share his zeal, all of us gathered today for the festival of his holy commemoration, all who admire his venerable life, and all who celebrate his blessed falling asleep in faith, by the grace and love of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom to the Father be glory, honor, and might, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
baehrens: PG 93; In sanctum Antonium (Khazarzar) u01 rem close
orientation: Hesychius keeps applying words from Hebrews to Antony and then ends the homily with a call to imitate him by the grace of Christ.
